worldPeriods.name: Old Kingdom Egypt
worldPeriods.note: The pyramid age — Djoser, Khufu, Khafre.

worldPeriods.name: Middle Kingdom Egypt
worldPeriods.note: Reunification after the First Intermediate Period.

worldPeriods.name: New Kingdom Egypt
worldPeriods.note: Egypt at its imperial peak — Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Ramesses II.

worldPeriods.name: Late Period & Ptolemaic Egypt
worldPeriods.note: Foreign and then Macedonian rule, ending with Cleopatra VII.

worldPeriods.name: Early Dynastic Sumer
worldPeriods.note: The first cities and the first writing, in Mesopotamia.

worldPeriods.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
worldPeriods.note: The largest empire the world had yet seen.

worldPeriods.name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
worldPeriods.note: Greece's great rival power through the Classical period.

worldPeriods.name: Roman Kingdom
worldPeriods.note: Seven legendary kings, ending with Tarquin the Proud.

worldPeriods.name: Roman Republic
worldPeriods.note: The power that eventually absorbed the entire Greek world.

worldPeriods.name: Carthage
worldPeriods.note: A Phoenician colony that grew into the western Mediterranean's dominant naval power, until Rome broke it.

worldPeriods.name: Indus Valley Civilisation
worldPeriods.note: Planned cities at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, with a still-undeciphered script.

worldPeriods.name: Vedic Civilisation
worldPeriods.note: The oral Vedas are composed; the foundations of classical Indian culture.

worldPeriods.name: Shang Dynasty China
worldPeriods.note: The first Chinese dynasty attested by contemporary writing — oracle bones.

worldPeriods.name: Zhou Dynasty China
worldPeriods.note: China's longest dynasty, spanning the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods.

worldEvents.name: Unification of Egypt
worldEvents.note: Traditional date for Narmer uniting Upper and Lower Egypt.

worldEvents.name: Great Pyramid of Giza completed
worldEvents.note: Built for Khufu — the last surviving Ancient Wonder.

worldEvents.name: Hyksos rule northern Egypt
worldEvents.note: Foreign Levantine rulers control the Nile Delta.

worldEvents.name: Hatshepsut's reign begins
worldEvents.note: One of the few women to rule Egypt as pharaoh in her own right.

worldEvents.name: Battle of Kadesh
worldEvents.note: Ramesses II vs. the Hittites — the earliest peace treaty to survive dates from its aftermath.

worldEvents.name: Rosetta Stone inscribed
worldEvents.note: Ptolemaic Egypt, trilingual decree — the eventual key to reading hieroglyphs.

worldEvents.name: Cleopatra VII becomes queen
worldEvents.note: The last Ptolemaic ruler, and the last pharaoh of independent Egypt.

worldEvents.name: Hammurabi's Code
worldEvents.note: One of the earliest and most complete written legal codes.

worldEvents.name: Fall of Nineveh
worldEvents.note: The Assyrian capital falls to a Babylonian-Median alliance — empire ends.

worldEvents.name: Cyrus the Great founds the Persian Empire
worldEvents.note: Conquers the Median Empire; Persia becomes the dominant power on Greece's doorstep.

worldEvents.name: Fall of Babylon to Cyrus
worldEvents.note: The Persian Empire absorbs Mesopotamia.

worldEvents.name: Founding of Rome (traditional)
worldEvents.note: The legendary date given by Roman historians themselves.

worldEvents.name: Rome becomes a Republic
worldEvents.note: The last king expelled; power passes to elected consuls.

worldEvents.name: Gauls sack Rome
worldEvents.note: A trauma Roman memory returned to for centuries.

worldEvents.name: Julius Caesar assassinated
worldEvents.note: The Republic's final crisis begins.

worldEvents.name: Augustus becomes first Roman Emperor
worldEvents.note: The Republic formally ends — three years before this dataset's own close.

worldEvents.name: Founding of Carthage (traditional)
worldEvents.note: Legendary founding by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, led by Dido.

worldEvents.name: First Punic War begins
worldEvents.note: Rome and Carthage fight for Sicily — the start of Roman naval power.

worldEvents.name: Hannibal crosses the Alps
worldEvents.note: The opening move of the Second Punic War.

worldEvents.name: Battle of Zama
worldEvents.note: Scipio defeats Hannibal — Carthage broken as a power.

worldEvents.name: Destruction of Carthage
worldEvents.note: The same year Rome also sacked Corinth — 146 BC ends Carthaginian and old Greek independence together.

worldEvents.name: Mature Harappan phase begins
worldEvents.note: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa reach their planned, standardised height.

worldEvents.name: Decline of the Indus cities
worldEvents.note: Urban centres are gradually abandoned; causes remain debated.

worldEvents.name: Shang oracle-bone script in use
worldEvents.note: The earliest confirmed form of Chinese writing, used for royal divination.

worldEvents.name: Confucius
worldEvents.note: Born during the Zhou dynasty's Spring and Autumn period; his teachings shape Chinese thought for millennia.

worldTerritories.name: Roman Empire
worldTerritories.label: Roman Empire
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: A single schematic outline for five centuries of an empire whose real borders moved constantly (this shape leans toward its 2nd-century AD extent). Seed data for the known-world overview — not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Roman Britain
worldTerritories.label: Roman Britain
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: Drawn separately from wt-roman-empire's mainland shape because Britain is a real island, not an artifact of this map's geometry -- and because Roman control never crossed the Irish Sea to Ireland, which a single box spanning both would otherwise have implied. Roughly the extent south of Hadrian's Wall, the empire's practical northern frontier for most of the occupation. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Early Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.label: Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: The eastern Roman state after the western empire's collapse, at its broadest — including Justinian's 6th-century reconquest of Italy and the North African coast, itself temporary and unevenly held. Seed data for the known-world overview — not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Middle Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.label: Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: After the 7th-century Arab conquests stripped away Egypt, the Levant and North Africa, the empire's core settled into Anatolia and the Balkans — itself contested and shifting across five and a half centuries. Seed data for the known-world overview — not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Late Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.label: Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: After the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204, the restored empire never recovered its former extent — by the 15th century it was little more than the capital and its immediate hinterland, encircled by Ottoman territory. Seed data for the known-world overview — not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Rashidun Caliphate
worldTerritories.label: Rashidun Caliphate
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: A single schematic outline for the fastest territorial expansion in this dataset -- from Arabia to the edge of Central Asia in under 30 years. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Umayyad Caliphate
worldTerritories.label: Umayyad Caliphate
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: The eastern two-thirds of the Umayyad Caliphate at its broadest extent (the Levant to Sindh, plus Arabia) -- reached in stages over this period, not held at this size throughout it. Iberia and the Maghreb are drawn separately as wt-umayyad-west, since a single ring cannot cleanly trace both this core and that western extension without crossing itself. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Umayyad Egypt
worldTerritories.label: Umayyad Caliphate
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: Drawn separately from wt-umayyad-west (Iberia and the Maghreb, which connects to it only through open desert, not a coastline this map can trace) and from wt-umayyad-caliphate (the Levant-to-Sindh core, on the Sinai's far side). Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Umayyad Caliphate (Iberia & the Maghreb)
worldTerritories.label: Umayyad Caliphate
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: The western third of the Umayyad Caliphate -- Iberia (conquered from 711) and North Africa west of Egypt -- drawn as its own shape rather than joined to wt-umayyad-caliphate's Levant-to-Sindh core, since a single ring cannot trace both without crossing itself. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Abbasid Caliphate
worldTerritories.label: Abbasid Caliphate
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: The Levant-to-Sindh core, plus Arabia; excludes Iberia (an independent Umayyad emirate from 756) and the far Maghreb (independent under the Idrisids from 789 and other local dynasties) -- those are covered, as far as Ifriqiya, by wt-abbasid-west, since a single ring cannot trace both without crossing itself. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Abbasid Egypt
worldTerritories.label: Abbasid Caliphate
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: Drawn separately from wt-abbasid-west (Ifriqiya, connected to it only through Cyrenaica's largely uncontrolled desert coast) and from wt-abbasid-height (the Levant-to-Sindh core). Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Abbasid Caliphate (Ifriqiya & Egypt)
worldTerritories.label: Abbasid Caliphate
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: The Abbasids' westernmost holdings -- Ifriqiya (roughly modern Tunisia) and Egypt -- drawn separately from wt-abbasid-height's Levant-to-Sindh core since a single ring cannot trace both without crossing itself. Morocco and the central Maghreb are excluded as independent under the Idrisids (from 789) and other local dynasties. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Abbasid Caliphate (reduced)
worldTerritories.label: Abbasid Caliphate
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: By the 10th century the Abbasid caliph's direct rule had shrunk to Mesopotamia and western Persia, and after the Buyid occupation of Baghdad in 945 to little more than the city itself, even as the caliph retained nominal religious authority across a much wider Islamic world now ruled by breakaway dynasties (Fatimids, Buyids, Samanids and others). Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Fatimid Caliphate
worldTerritories.label: Fatimid Caliphate
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: A Shia caliphate ruling in competition with the Abbasids, at its broadest extent after taking Egypt in 969 -- Levantine and Hejaz control fluctuated and was not held continuously across this whole window. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Crusader States (at their height)
worldTerritories.label: Crusader States
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: The County of Edessa, Principality of Antioch, County of Tripoli and Kingdom of Jerusalem shown as one combined coastal outline rather than four separately governed states -- a real simplification of a patchwork under nominally allied but independent Latin rulers. Ends at Saladin's victory at Hattin. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Crusader States (after Hattin)
worldTerritories.label: Crusader States
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: After Saladin's victory at Hattin in 1187 the Crusader states lost Jerusalem and most of their inland territory, surviving as a narrow Acre-centred coastal strip (plus Tripoli and Antioch's own remnants) until the fall of Acre in 1291. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Sultanate of Rum
worldTerritories.label: Sultanate of Rum
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: Seljuk Turkic rule over most of Anatolia, established after the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert in 1071 and fragmenting after the Mongol victory at Kose Dag in 1243 into the small competing beyliks (including the nascent Ottoman one) that the Sultanate nominally, then barely, held together until 1308. Bridges the gap between Byzantine Anatolia and Ottoman Anatolia. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Ottoman Empire (rising)
worldTerritories.label: Ottoman Empire
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: From a small beylik around Sogut (1300) to control of northwestern Anatolia and, after crossing into Europe in 1354, Thrace, Macedonia and Bulgaria -- growth that happened in stages across this window, not as one stable border. Ends at the Ottoman defeat by Timur at Ankara in 1402. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Ottoman Empire (recovery to conquest)
worldTerritories.label: Ottoman Empire
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: From the civil wars following Timur's victory at Ankara through the recovery under Mehmed I and Murad II to Mehmed II's capture of Constantinople in 1453 -- by which point Ottoman territory encircled the Byzantine capital almost completely. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Elam
worldTerritories.label: Elam
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: A single schematic outline for over two thousand years of a state whose real borders and periods of strength fluctuated substantially, capital at Susa throughout. Ends with the Achaemenid conquest. Seed data for the known-world overview -- not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldSites.name: Nineveh
worldSites.note: The Neo-Assyrian capital under Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal, on the Tigris opposite modern Mosul. The mounds of Kuyunjik and Nabi Yunus preserve palace and temple remains; excavation resumed in 2019 after ISIL-era destruction, and an archaeological park opened in 2023.

worldSites.name: Nimrud
worldSites.note: Ancient Kalhu, made the Assyrian imperial capital by Ashurnasirpal II. Roughly 90% of its excavated palaces and its ziggurat were destroyed by ISIL in 2015; UNESCO-backed restoration has been under way since 2017.

worldSites.name: Ashur
worldSites.note: Political capital of the Middle Assyrian kingdom and, even after the court moved elsewhere, Assyria's religious capital -- seat of the god Ashur -- until the city was destroyed in 614 BC. Temple, ziggurat and palace ruins survive on the Tigris; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003.

worldSites.name: Khorsabad (Dur-Sharrukin)
worldSites.note: A purpose-built royal city -- "Fortress of Sargon" -- constructed from scratch by Sargon II as his new capital and abandoned almost immediately after his death. Walls and gates are partly reconstructed; excavation resumed in 2023 after ISIL-era looting.

worldSites.name: Ur
worldSites.note: A Sumerian city-state, briefly the largest city in the world under the Third Dynasty of Ur (c. 2112-2004 BC). Its stepped ziggurat, dedicated to the moon god Nanna, is the best-preserved in Mesopotamia; the royal cemetery yielded the site's richest Bronze Age finds.

worldSites.name: Uruk
worldSites.note: The largest city in the world around 3100 BC, with a population estimated near 50,000, and the setting most associated with the invention of writing. The Eanna and Anu temple precincts survive as a large tell; the site remained occupied for millennia afterward.

worldSites.name: Nippur
worldSites.note: Sumer's paramount religious centre -- home to the temple of the chief god Enlil -- rather than a political capital in its own right; rulers across Mesopotamia sought legitimacy through building work here. The temple tell has been under renewed joint excavation since 2025.

worldSites.name: Susa
worldSites.note: Capital of Elam for two millennia, then one of the Achaemenid Persian Empire's four capitals alongside Persepolis, Pasargadae and Ecbatana. The Apadana palace mound and citadel survive beside modern Shush; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015.

worldSites.name: Pasargadae
worldSites.note: The first Achaemenid capital, built by Cyrus the Great after his victory over the Medes; its palace and garden complex survive, along with Cyrus's own tomb nearby. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2004.

worldSites.name: Ecbatana
worldSites.note: Capital of the Median Empire, then the Achaemenid Persian kings' summer capital. The ancient mound, Hagmatana Tepe, lies mostly buried beneath modern Hamadan, which has limited excavation to occasional, small seasons.

worldSites.name: Sardis
worldSites.note: Capital of the Lydian kingdom under Gyges and Croesus, captured by Cyrus the Great in 546 BC and afterward a major Achaemenid satrapal seat. Excavations since 1958 have exposed a large gymnasium-synagogue complex, a Temple of Artemis and royal tumuli.

worldSites.name: Gordion
worldSites.note: Capital of Phrygia, associated with King Midas; its citadel mound and royal burial tumuli (including the so-called "Midas Mound") have been under active excavation since the 1950s. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.

worldSites.name: Carchemish
worldSites.note: A major Hittite, then Neo-Hittite, city on the Euphrates straddling the modern Turkey-Syria border, conquered by Sargon II in 717 BC. Its citadel and lower town reopened as an archaeological park in 2019 after decades inaccessible along the border.

worldSites.name: Damascus
worldSites.note: One of the longest continuously inhabited cities in the world; capital of the Umayyad Caliphate (661-750) and still a major provincial capital under the Mamluks and Ottomans. The walled Old City, including the Umayyad Mosque, survives on the Roman-era street grid.

worldSites.name: Jerusalem
worldSites.note: Continuously significant across Israelite, Babylonian, Persian, Roman, Byzantine, early Islamic, Crusader and Mamluk rule -- captured by the First Crusade in 1099 and made capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem until Saladin retook it in 1187. The walled Old City contains the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Western Wall.

worldSites.name: Ctesiphon
worldSites.note: Capital of the Parthian and then Sasanian Persian empires for nearly 900 years, until its capture by Arab Muslim armies in 637. Taq Kasra, the great Sasanian audience-hall arch, is the only major structure still standing above ground.

worldSites.name: Baghdad
worldSites.note: Founded in 762 by the caliph al-Mansur as a purpose-built circular capital, "the Round City" -- nothing of it survives above ground today, fully overbuilt by the later city. The Abbasid golden age centred here until the Mongol sack of 1258, after which Baghdad continued as a provincial city.

worldSites.name: Mecca
worldSites.note: A pre-Islamic sanctuary town that became Islam's holiest city after Muhammad's conquest in 630. The Kaaba, at the centre of the Masjid al-Haram, is the focal point of Muslim pilgrimage; the caliphate's political centre moved elsewhere almost immediately, to Medina and then Damascus.

worldSites.name: Medina
worldSites.note: Muhammad's destination in the Hijra of 622, which marks the start of the Islamic calendar, and the seat of the caliphate under the first four ("Rightly Guided") caliphs until 661. Al-Masjid al-Nabawi, built by Muhammad himself, includes his tomb.

worldSites.name: Fustat
worldSites.note: Egypt's first Arab-Islamic capital, founded by the general Amr ibn al-As in 641 after the Byzantine province fell to Muslim armies. Superseded as capital in 969 when the Fatimids founded al-Qahira (Cairo) just to its north; the Mosque of Amr and the old Coptic quarter survive in what is now Old Cairo.

worldSites.name: Córdoba
worldSites.note: Capital of Islamic al-Andalus, first as an independent Umayyad emirate (756, founded by a prince who escaped the Abbasid revolution) and then as a caliphate in its own right (929-1031). The Mezquita, its former congregational mosque, survives -- consecrated as a cathedral after the Christian reconquest of the city in 1236.

worldSites.name: Kairouan
worldSites.note: The first Islamic city founded in the Maghreb, in 670, and a base for the subsequent Arab conquest of North Africa and Iberia. Its Great Mosque, founded the same year and rebuilt several times since, is the oldest in the Maghreb; the city declined after Bedouin invasions in the 11th century.

worldSites.name: Edessa
worldSites.note: Seat of the County of Edessa, the first and most exposed of the Crusader states, established in 1098. Its fall to the Muslim ruler of Aleppo in 1144 shocked Europe and prompted the Second Crusade. The citadel and the Pool of Abraham survive in modern Sanliurfa.

worldSites.name: Tripoli
worldSites.note: Seat of the County of Tripoli, the last of the four Crusader states to be established (1109) and the last to fall, sacked by the Mamluks in 1289. The Crusader-era city stood nearer the coast; after its destruction the rebuilt Mamluk city (whose citadel survives) rose about 3 km inland.

worldSites.name: Acre
worldSites.note: Capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem after Saladin retook Jerusalem itself in 1187, and the last major Crusader stronghold -- its fall to the Mamluks in 1291 ended Latin Christian rule in the Levant. Crusader-era substructures survive beneath the later Ottoman old city.

worldSites.name: Bursa
worldSites.note: The first permanent Ottoman capital, captured from the Byzantines in 1326 and held until Edirne succeeded it in 1369. The tombs of the early sultans and the Green Mosque/Tomb complex survive; a UNESCO World Heritage Site as the "birthplace of the Ottoman Empire."

worldSites.name: Edirne
worldSites.note: Ancient Adrianople; the second Ottoman capital, held from 1369 until Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453. Its old Ottoman core predates the later Selimiye Mosque, built after the events shown on this map.

worldSites.name: Ravenna
worldSites.note: Capital of the Western Roman Empire from 402, then of Odoacer's and the Ostrogoths' Italian kingdoms, then -- after Justinian's reconquest -- of Byzantine Italy as the seat of the Exarchate until the Lombards captured it in 751. Its Roman and Byzantine mosaics (San Vitale, Sant'Apollinare Nuovo) are the best preserved anywhere.

worldSites.name: Trebizond
worldSites.note: Capital of the Empire of Trebizond, a Byzantine successor state founded after the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204. It outlasted the restored Byzantine Empire itself, falling to the Ottomans in 1461, eight years after Constantinople. Its walls and the Hagia Sophia of Trebizond survive.
